Pugnacious

pug-NAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Pugnacious is eager or quick to argue or fight.

The pugnacious boxer talked trash to every opponent before a single punch was ever thrown.

Worked Example

The pugnacious toddler squared up to his own shadow, ready to fight anything that moved.

Pugnacious describes a personality trait -- a readiness to argue or fight -- not a single angry outburst.

How Pugnacious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

argumentative

argumentative: given to quarreling or arguing

scrappy

scrappy: the everyday word for feisty, good-natured fighting spirit; pugnacious is the more formal word for being quick to argue or fight

Antonyms

peaceable

peaceable: inclined to avoid conflict

easygoing

easygoing: friendly and good-tempered

How Strong Is It? — assertive → pugnacious → hostile

assertive vs. pugnacious

assertive vs. pugnacious: Assertive simply means confidently expressing oneself; pugnacious goes further, implying an eagerness for actual conflict.

hostile vs. pugnacious

hostile vs. pugnacious: Hostile goes further than pugnacious, implying open antagonism, not just a readiness to argue.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of pugnacious.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — pugn

root — pugn: to fight (Latin (pugnare))

suffix — -acious

suffix — -acious: full of, inclined to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: pugn- ('to fight') + -acious ('full of, inclined to') together mean 'full of fighting' -- quick to argue or fight.

Use the root in a new word: repugnant

Use the root in a new word: repugnant: Repugnant shares the same Latin root pugnare ('to fight'), taught earlier in Unit 52 -- though repugnant has come to mean 'deeply offensive' rather than 'ready to fight.'
